sentence: A panic attack causes physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat, dizziness, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath, along with a sense of dread.
The NHS says a panic attack usually passes within minutes, and that fighting it often makes it worse.
note: NHS: usually 5 to 20 minutes; fighting can make it worse (other NHS source).

sentence: Cognitive behavioural therapy is the main talking therapy for repeated panic attacks, and NHS talking therapies accept self-referral.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear or anxiety.
note: NHS description; flagged for second pass.

sentence: A single panic attack does not necessarily mean someone has panic disorder, which is when attacks keep coming back.
note: Retrieved: single attack does not necessarily mean panic disorder.

sentence: Common physical signs are a racing heartbeat, dizziness, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath and nausea, along with a sense of dread.
The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes.
note: NHS: 5 to 20 minutes (NHS inform gives a slightly longer range).

sentence: Other symptoms the NHS lists include feeling faint, chest pain, hot flushes, chills, numbness or pins and needles, and a dry mouth.
Many of these symptoms overlap with those of other conditions, so a GP check is useful when attacks are new.
note: Search summary note; flagged for second pass.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales says that although panic attacks are frightening, they are not dangerous.
The NHS advice is to stay where you are if you can, breathe slowly and deeply, and remind yourself that the attack will pass and is not life threatening.
note: NHS: stay where you are, slow deep breaths, it will pass.

sentence: NHS Scotland notes that fighting a panic attack can often make it worse, so accepting the feeling tends to work better than resisting it.
note: NHS inform: fighting can make it worse.

sentence: Grounding techniques, such as focusing on the senses, can also help.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is the main psychological treatment, and people in England can refer themselves to a talking therapies service or ask a GP to refer them.
The NHS lists an SSRI antidepressant as the first medicine, with a tricyclic antidepressant if SSRIs are not suitable.
These medicines can take a few weeks to start working, and the NHS advises talking to the GP rather than stopping them without advice.
note: NHS: 2 to 4 weeks; do not stop without GP advice.

sentence: NICE says psychological therapy, medicine and self-help have all been shown to work, and that the benefits of psychological treatment lasted longest.
The exact cause of panic disorder is not fully understood, and NHS Scotland says it is probably a combination of physical and psychological factors.
A GP asks the person to describe the symptoms, how often they happen and how long they have lasted, and may carry out a physical examination to rule out other conditions.
The NHS suggests regular exercise, calming breathing practice, and cutting down on caffeine, sugary drinks, alcohol and smoking, which can make attacks worse.
It also advises against avoiding feared situations altogether, and recommends building up to them gradually.
The NHS says to speak to a GP if attacks keep happening or affect daily life.
If symptoms do not improve, a GP may refer someone to a mental health specialist.
Panic attacks are frightening but pass. If a person feels unable to stay safe, urgent help is open at any time.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
note: Samaritans 116 123 free, 24 hours: returned in the urgent-help and NHS grief searches.
